strengths: Timely and practically relevant topic: understanding how compression affects large reasoning models is important for deployment and accessibility.
The paper compares several compression families, including dynamic quantization, distillation, and pruning, rather than focusing on only one technique.
The benchmark suite spans multiple reasoning categories, including math, logic, temporal reasoning, and multihop QA, giving a useful first look at heterogeneous behavior.
The sparsity sweep for distilled models is informative and reveals plausible collapse regimes, especially the sharp degradation at high sparsity.

The observation that closed-book MuSiQue is more sensitive to parameter count than some reasoning-only tasks is interesting and could motivate future work on separating knowledge retention from reasoning ability.
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily a small-scale empirical benchmark with limited methodological novelty; it does not introduce a new compression method, evaluation protocol, or strong theoretical insight.

The evaluation is too limited for strong claims: AIME 2024 has only 30 questions, MuSiQue is subsampled to 100 examples, all evaluations use a single pass, and there are no confidence intervals or significance tests.

The comparisons are not fully controlled. Original DeepSeek-R1 is evaluated through an API while quantized models are run locally, and the authors report repeated prompting after empty API responses, which raises concerns about comparability and selection bias.
The paper omits central compression metrics such as actual memory usage, latency, throughput, energy, and hardware requirements, even though deployment efficiency is a core motivation.

The test-time compute analysis is correlational and likely confounded: shorter responses may correspond to easier questions or higher model confidence. The paper does not establish that reducing verbosity would causally improve reasoning accuracy.
Token counting is done by treating words as tokens rather than using model tokenizers, weakening the precision of the test-time compute analysis.
Reproducibility is incomplete: prompts, exact sampled MuSiQue instances, extraction rules, handling of invalid outputs, hardware setup, and pruning calibration details are not sufficiently specified.
The paper makes broad recommendations, such as preferring quantization when parametric knowledge is needed, from a narrow set of models and tasks.

Some baselines are missing or underdeveloped, such as other quantization methods, smaller non-distilled reasoning models, retrieval-augmented settings for MuSiQue, and comparisons to standard non-reasoning compressed LLMs.
Several claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially claims about parameter count affecting knowledge more than reasoning and shorter reasoning chains improving performance.

strengths: The paper studies a timely and practically relevant question: how compressed large reasoning models behave on reasoning benchmarks, especially given the high deployment cost of DeepSeek-R1-scale models.
The scope covers several compression families, including quantization, distillation, and pruning, and the paper reports results across mathematical, logical, temporal, and multihop QA tasks.

The empirical observation that aggressive pruning can lead to repetitive generation and collapse is useful, and the tables provide a compact first-pass comparison of several publicly available R1 variants.
weaknesses: The contribution is mainly a small empirical benchmark rather than a new method or deep analysis, and the novelty is limited for a top-tier AI venue. Most evaluated models are existing released models, and SparseGPT is an existing pruning method applied to distilled variants.

The evaluation is too thin to support the broad claims. AIME has only 30 questions, MuSiQue is reduced to 100 sampled questions, all benchmarks are single-pass, and there is no variance, confidence interval, or significance analysis.

The comparison between original R1 and quantized R1 is not well controlled. The original R1 is accessed via API while quantized models are run locally with llama.cpp; the authors also report empty API responses and iterative reprompting, which makes the baseline unreliable and weakens claims such as 2.51-bit R1 outperforming R1.

The central conclusion that parameter count affects knowledge much more than reasoning is not convincingly established. It is inferred from a very small set of models and is heavily confounded by architecture, training data, distillation recipe, tokenizer, and benchmark choice.

The test-time compute analysis is methodologically weak. Shorter outputs likely correspond to easier questions or higher model confidence, so the paper cannot conclude that reducing verbosity improves reasoning performance from this correlation alone. Counting words rather than model tokens also undermines the compute interpretation.

Important implementation details are missing or underspecified, including prompts, answer extraction rules, SparseGPT calibration data and hyperparameters, sampling seed for MuSiQue, repeated prompting protocol for API failures, and exact versions of model checkpoints and inference engines.

The paper evaluates compression but largely omits the main practical quantities motivating compression: memory footprint, latency, throughput, hardware requirements, and actual inference cost under comparable serving conditions.

Baselines and positioning are incomplete. The paper does not compare against other quantization schemes, structured pruning methods, smaller non-distilled reasoning models, closed-book retrieval alternatives, or standard evaluation harnesses under matched settings.

The benchmark selection is uneven. Temporal Sequences saturates near 100% for many models and is not very informative, while MuSiQue in closed-book mode mixes reasoning with memorization in a way that makes interpretation difficult.

The writing and analysis contain overclaims and some quality issues, including treating benchmark difficulty as inferred from only a few model scores, drawing recommendations from narrow evidence, and presenting compressed tables with formatting problems that make results hard to audit.

strengths: Timely and useful empirical focus: compressed large reasoning models are under-studied, and benchmarking DeepSeek-R1 variants across quantization, distillation, and pruning is relevant to deployment and democratization of LRMs.

The paper covers several reasoning categories rather than relying only on standard language modeling/perplexity metrics, including mathematical, logical, temporal, and multihop/knowledge-intensive QA tasks.

The comparison across quantized R1, distilled R1, and sparsified distilled models yields practically useful observations, especially that low-bit quantization appears to preserve performance better than distillation/pruning when parametric knowledge matters.
The sparsity sweep is informative: evaluating multiple pruning levels exposes collapse behavior and shows that the collapse point depends on benchmark difficulty.
The test-time compute analysis is an interesting addition and highlights a potentially important phenomenon: unusually long reasoning traces often correlate with worse answers.
weaknesses: The main contribution is primarily benchmarking rather than a new method or benchmark, so the novelty is moderate for a top-tier AI venue.

Evaluation reliability is limited by small sample sizes and single-pass inference: AIME has only 30 examples, MuSiQue is subsampled to 100 examples, and no confidence intervals, statistical tests, or multiple seeds/runs are reported.

The comparison between original R1 and quantized R1 is potentially confounded because R1 is evaluated through an API while quantized models use local inference; the authors note empty API responses, but this weakens claims that quantized R1 can outperform the original.

The paper does not report core compression/deployment metrics such as memory footprint, latency, throughput, hardware requirements, or cost, even though these are central motivations for model compression.

The claim that parameter count affects knowledge memorization more than reasoning is plausible but not fully isolated: model family, distillation data, pretraining corpus, quantization method, and pruning procedure are all confounded with parameter count.

The test-time compute conclusion is correlational and may be partly explained by harder questions inducing longer outputs; the paper does not control for item difficulty or perform interventions that force concise versus verbose reasoning.

Reproducibility is incomplete: prompts, exact decoding details beyond high-level settings, sampled MuSiQue question IDs, answer extraction rules, handling of empty/refusal outputs, and code are not sufficiently specified.

Some baselines are missing or narrow, such as other quantization methods, other LRMs, non-R1 compressed reasoning models, RAG settings for MuSiQue, and comparisons to similarly sized non-distilled models.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: how compression affects large reasoning models, with practical relevance for deploying DeepSeek-R1-style models under memory constraints.

The empirical scope is broader than many compression papers: it compares quantization, distillation, and pruning across several model sizes and multiple reasoning benchmarks, including math, logical, temporal, and multihop QA settings.

The paper makes a useful attempt to connect benchmark degradation with component-level analysis, using steering-vector/attribution-patching style scores rather than only reporting aggregate accuracies.

Some findings are actionable, especially the observation that aggressive pruning and 3-bit quantization hurt difficult reasoning tasks much more than 4-bit quantization, and that preserving final-layer MLP components may improve low-bit quantization.
The paper is generally well organized, and the main tables make the performance tradeoffs among compression methods easy to inspect.
weaknesses: The strongest claims are over-generalized relative to the evidence. The headline result that protecting about 2% of weights improves accuracy by 6.57% is validated only for 3-bit AWQ on R1-Distill-Llama-8B, with no replication on Qwen, larger distilled models, GPTQ/GPTAQ/ANY3, or dynamically quantized R1.

The interpretability analysis is not sufficiently validated to support causal claims about which weights are responsible for reasoning. The paper relies on GPT-4o-labeled behavior spans, but does not report labeling prompts, validation accuracy, human agreement, sensitivity to span choices, or robustness across prompts/datasets.

The attribution-patching evidence is treated as causal, but the validation is narrow: selectively quantizing only five components in one model is not enough to establish that the importance scores reliably identify critical reasoning weights. There are no random-component, matched-size, or alternative-score baselines.

The benchmark evaluation has statistical limitations. AIME 2024 has only 30 examples, MuSiQue is subsampled to 100 examples, and many reported differences are small, yet the paper provides no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance estimates beyond averaging some runs.

The evaluation protocol is inconsistent across model families: DeepSeek-R1 and dynamically quantized models are evaluated differently from other models, and some pruning tables use one-pass scores. This weakens comparisons among compression strategies.

The knowledge-versus-reasoning conclusion is under-supported. Closed-book MuSiQue performance is extremely low for many models and conflates parametric knowledge, answer formatting, retrieval absence, and multihop reasoning; using it as the main basis for claims about knowledge retention is fragile.

The mixed-precision protection experiment lacks essential baselines, such as protecting random final-layer weights, protecting the same number of weights in other modules, protecting components selected by AWQ saliency, or comparing against established mixed-precision quantization methods under the same bit budget.

The paper does not analyze latency, memory, throughput, or effective compression after selective 16-bit protection, despite making deployment-motivated claims. Compression ratio and practical efficiency are therefore not fully characterized.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript: implementation details for behavior extraction, calibration data, quantization settings, prompts, parsing rules, and code availability are either missing or too vague for confident replication.

Related work positioning could be sharper. Some observations, such as final layers being sensitive or 4-bit quantization being relatively robust, are plausible extensions of known LLM compression behavior, so the novelty of the mechanistic findings needs stronger empirical support.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important question: how quantization, pruning, and distillation affect large reasoning models rather than general-purpose LLMs.
It compares several compression families and multiple quantization methods on DeepSeek-R1 and distilled R1 variants, giving a useful empirical snapshot of current compressed reasoning models.

The attempt to connect benchmark degradation with module-level importance is interesting, and the selective final-layer protection experiment suggests a potentially useful direction for mixed-precision quantization.
weaknesses: The central interpretability claims are not technically convincing. The paper treats difference-of-means steering vectors plus attribution patching as identifying causal weight importance, but the approximation is weakly justified and only lightly validated.

Reasoning-behavior labels are produced by GPT-4o, yet there is no rigorous validation of label quality, inter-annotator agreement, sensitivity analysis, or evidence that the labeled spans correspond to the claimed mechanisms.

Several major conclusions are overclaimed. For example, comparing importance shifts between a distilled model and its base model is not sufficient to conclude that final-layer importance is caused by distillation, and the claim that specific modules are 'overly compressed' is not established causally.

The evaluation is narrow and statistically fragile: AIME 2024 has only 30 examples, MuSiQue uses only 100 sampled examples, Temporal is nearly saturated for many models, and the paper provides little uncertainty analysis beyond averaging some runs.

The strongest practical claim, that protecting 2% of weights improves 3-bit quantization by 6.57%, is shown only for one model and one protection choice. There are no strong controls such as random module protection, protection of equally sized alternative modules, or comparisons under fixed memory/latency budgets.

The compression comparison is uneven. Dynamic quantized full R1 models, distilled models, post-training quantized models, and SparseGPT-pruned models differ greatly in scale, implementation, inference backend, and compression ratio, making some cross-method takeaways difficult to interpret.

The pruning analysis is limited to SparseGPT on two distilled models and mostly documents degradation. This is not enough to support broad claims about pruning or knowledge retention under compression.

The paper does not evaluate inference speed, latency, throughput, calibration cost, memory footprint under the proposed mixed-precision protection, or deployment tradeoffs, despite framing compression as an efficiency problem.

Reproducibility is incomplete: key details about prompts, parsing, calibration data, sampled MuSiQue questions, GPT-4o labeling protocol, and interpretability implementation are insufficiently specified in the main paper.

Writing and presentation contain rough edges and some imprecise wording, and the paper’s claims are often stronger than the evidence supports. Overall, the work is plausible but not competitive for a top-tier AI conference in its current form.

strengths: Timely and relevant problem: understanding how quantization, distillation, and pruning affect large reasoning models is important for practical deployment and underexplored relative to general LLM compression.
The paper combines broad empirical benchmarking with mechanistic analysis, giving a more informative picture than accuracy-only compression studies.
The evaluation covers multiple compression families and several R1/R1-distilled model scales, including AWQ, GPTQ, GPTAQ, ANY3/4, SparseGPT, and Unsloth dynamic quantization.
Several findings are concrete and potentially useful for future compression work, especially the emphasis on final-layer MLP modules and gate projections as sensitive components.
The authors attempt to validate interpretability-derived importance scores through targeted quantization/protection experiments, which strengthens the paper beyond purely post-hoc heatmap analysis.
The presentation is generally clear, with well-organized takeaways and useful tables summarizing performance trends across compression settings.
weaknesses: The main mechanistic claims are stronger than the evidence supports. The attribution-patching-style importance scores are only lightly validated, mostly on R1-Distill-Llama-8B and a small number of module interventions, so it is unclear how robust the conclusions are across models, tasks, prompts, and compression methods.

The reasoning-behavior labels rely on GPT-4o token-sequence annotation, but the paper does not sufficiently establish annotation quality, agreement, sensitivity to labeling errors, or whether the four selected behaviors adequately represent reasoning capability.

The comparison between distilled models and their base backbones is difficult to interpret causally: differences may reflect instruction tuning, data, architecture/backbone effects, or distribution shift, not distillation alone. The claim that important weights are mainly the result of distillation is therefore somewhat under-supported.

The evaluation suite is useful but limited. AIME 2024 has only 30 examples, MuSiQue uses a random sample of 100 in a closed-book setting, and there is little statistical uncertainty analysis beyond averaging some runs.

The pruning analysis is relatively shallow compared with quantization and distillation: only SparseGPT on two large distilled models is studied, and pruning is mostly dropped from later interpretation after observing collapse.

The mixed-precision protection result is promising but not yet a convincing state-of-the-art claim. Keeping selected modules in 16-bit changes the effective bit budget, and the method is only demonstrated for 3-bit AWQ on one 8B model; stronger comparisons to existing mixed-precision or sensitivity-aware quantization methods are needed.

Efficiency is not evaluated beyond compression ratios. Since deployment is a motivating goal, memory footprint, throughput, latency, and hardware implications would help establish practical significance.

Reproducibility details appear incomplete in the main paper, including exact prompts, calibration data, extraction/labeling protocol, random seeds, and full code availability for the interpretation pipeline.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant question: how compression affects large reasoning models, with a useful side-by-side look at quantization, distillation, and pruning.
The empirical benchmark covers multiple model families, model sizes, and compression methods, including dynamic quantization, AWQ, GPTQ, GPTAQ, ANY, SparseGPT, and AlphaPruning.

The fine-grained module-level interpretability analysis is interesting and potentially useful for compression research, especially the focus on identifying modules whose importance shifts after compression.
The paper attempts to validate interpretability-derived claims with interventions, such as selectively quantizing the final-layer up projection and protecting final-layer MLP modules.
The writing is generally clear, and the paper gives concrete takeaways rather than only reporting benchmark tables.
weaknesses: The main claims are stronger than the evidence. Generalization claims across LRMs and non-R1 models are based on a small number of models and limited interventions, with most causal validation concentrated on R1-distilled Llama-8B and AWQ/GPTQ variants.

The benchmark suite is relatively narrow and statistically fragile. AIME 2024 has only 30 examples, MuSiQue is sampled to 100 examples, and several important rows are one-pass or not repeated, yet the paper draws broad conclusions about collapse points and knowledge retention.

The comparison between compression methods is not fully controlled. Dynamic R1 quantization, distillation, pruning, and quantization are applied to different base architectures, parameter counts, calibration data, and inference stacks, making some conclusions about relative compression strategies hard to isolate.

The interpretability pipeline depends on GPT-4o annotations of reasoning behaviors over only 120 instances, and the robustness check is weak: only 10 sampled instances per behavior are human-scored, with wide confidence intervals for some behaviors.

The attribution-patching importance scores are treated as causal module importance, but the causal validity is only partially established. Selective quantization is a coarse perturbation that may introduce distributional artifacts rather than cleanly measuring reasoning behavior dependence.

The proposed protection result is promising but underdeveloped: it is shown mainly for 3-bit AWQ on one model, with no comparison to standard mixed-precision allocation baselines, no memory/speed tradeoff analysis, and limited evidence that the 6.57% gain is robust.

The paper explicitly omits inference speedup despite studying compression. This weakens the practical significance, since memory, latency, throughput, and hardware compatibility are central to compression claims.

Some conclusions about knowledge memorization versus reasoning are confounded by closed-book evaluation and model size. The MuSiQue results indicate poor factual recall, but do not cleanly separate memorization, retrieval failure, answer formatting, and reasoning ability.

Reproducibility is incomplete: exact prompts, calibration data, annotation prompts, intervention implementation details, and code/resources are not sufficiently specified in the main paper; the authors also note that calibration details for Unsloth quantization are unknown.

The novelty is moderate rather than strong. The paper is more of an empirical/interpretable analysis than a new compression method, and several findings are plausible extensions of known sensitivity of late layers and MLP modules in LLM compression.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important question: how quantization, distillation, and pruning affect large reasoning models, especially DeepSeek-R1 and distilled R1 variants.

The empirical scope is broader than many compression papers, covering several compression families, multiple model sizes, and several reasoning benchmarks rather than relying only on perplexity or simple end tasks.
The paper makes an effort to go beyond aggregate accuracy by proposing module-level analyses and validating some claims with targeted quantization/protection experiments.

Some observations are useful and plausible, such as 4-bit quantization often preserving reasoning performance better than aggressive pruning, and knowledge-heavy closed-book QA being more sensitive to parameter-count reduction.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claims are not sufficiently supported. The paper repeatedly describes module scores as causal weight importance, but the method relies on GPT-4o-labeled behavior spans, difference-of-means directions, gradients, and relative normalization; this is a weak basis for strong causal conclusions about which weights are responsible for reasoning.

The annotation pipeline is a major weakness. Reasoning behaviors are automatically labeled by GPT-4o, and the robustness check uses only 10 sampled instances per behavior with very wide confidence intervals; for adding knowledge, the reported Spearman interval includes negative correlation. This is inadequate for the interpretability claims.

The evaluation is too small and noisy for the strength of the conclusions. AIME 2024 has only 30 questions, MuSiQue uses only 100 sampled questions, many results are one-pass or not repeated for key models, and there is little statistical testing despite large variance in LRM outputs.

Comparisons across compression methods are not well controlled. Dynamic quantization, AWQ/GPTQ/GPTAQ/ANY, pruning, and distillation differ in model family, calibration data, inference backend, compression target, and bit allocation, making several aggregate comparisons difficult to interpret.

The claimed generalization beyond R1 is weak. The non-R1 evidence appears to rely mainly on one distilled GPT-OSS/Qwen model and one quantized variant, with one-pass benchmarking, which is far from enough to claim generality across non-R1 LRMs.

The selective validation experiments are not convincing enough. Quantizing or protecting one module can perturb model behavior in idiosyncratic ways, and the controls are limited. Some reported exceptions, such as layer 1 up-projection producing worse AIME results than the claimed most important module, are hand-waved as randomness rather than rigorously analyzed.

The paper’s strongest practical claim, that protecting about 2% of weights beats state-of-the-art 3-bit quantization by large margins, is demonstrated in a very narrow setting: one model, one protection rule, limited benchmarks, and no latency/memory/hardware analysis. The added full-precision weights may also complicate deployment but this is not evaluated.

The paper overstates several takeaways. For example, broad claims about knowledge memorization versus reasoning, final-layer up-projection importance, and compression bottlenecks are presented as general findings despite limited evidence and possible confounds from benchmark choice, decoding settings, and model families.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives implementation details, but does not appear to provide code, exact prompts, calibration data details for some methods, model checkpoints for modified quantization/protection runs, or sufficient information to reproduce the interpretability pipeline end to end.

The writing is understandable but often imprecise. Terms such as reasoning capability, knowledge memorization, importance, causal relationship, compression effect, and collapse are used in ways that sometimes exceed what the experiments actually establish.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and important problem: understanding how compression affects large reasoning models, rather than evaluating compressed LLMs only on perplexity or simple downstream tasks.

The scope is relatively broad across compression families, including distillation, dynamic quantization, AWQ, GPTQ, GPTAQ, ANY4/3, SparseGPT, and AlphaPruning, with evaluations on mathematical, logical, temporal, and knowledge-intensive reasoning tasks.

The combination of benchmarking with mechanistic analysis is a meaningful contribution. The module-level importance analysis provides useful hypotheses about which weights are critical for reasoning, especially final-layer MLP up projections and gate projections.

The authors do not stop at interpretability heatmaps: they provide empirical verification via selective quantization and selective protection, showing that protecting roughly 2% of weights can substantially improve 3-bit AWQ accuracy.

The results are practically relevant. The findings that weight count matters more for knowledge retention than reasoning, and that 3-bit quantization/pruning still have major bottlenecks, are useful for future LRM compression work.

The paper is generally clear, well organized, and includes helpful appendices with implementation details, additional visualizations, annotation robustness checks, RAG experiments, pruning analysis, and non-R1 generalization evidence.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence warrants. Attribution patching with GPT-4o-labeled behavior spans is useful, but still approximate; the paper sometimes treats these importance scores as causal evidence for weight-level reasoning mechanisms more confidently than justified.

The annotation validation is limited: only 120 instances are annotated, and the human robustness check samples only 10 instances per behavior. Some confidence intervals are wide, especially for adding knowledge, which weakens the interpretability conclusions.

The evaluation, while broad in compression methods, is fairly narrow in benchmark scale. AIME has only 30 questions, MuSiQue uses a 100-question sample, and several comparisons rely on one-pass scores or API/llama.cpp/vLLM differences, making some quantitative conclusions fragile.

The comparison across compression methods is not always apples-to-apples. Dynamic quantized R1, distilled dense models, and post-training quantized distilled models differ in architecture, calibration data, runtime stack, and compression target, which complicates claims about which compression strategy is best.

The paper explicitly does not evaluate inference speedup, memory throughput, or serving efficiency. Since compression is motivated by deployment cost, this leaves an important practical dimension unmeasured.
The generality claims remain somewhat overstated. Most main evidence is R1-centric, and the non-R1 validation is limited to one distilled GPT-OSS/Qwen-style model and one quantization setting.

The paper could more carefully separate knowledge retention, reasoning ability, and answer extraction reliability. Closed-book MuSiQue performance is suggestive, but stronger controls would be needed to fully support the claim that parameter count affects knowledge more than reasoning.

Reproducibility may be challenging without released code, prompts, model outputs, annotation data, calibration data, and exact quantization/pruning configurations, since the conclusions depend on many implementation-sensitive details.
